newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: ZAIRE'S MOBUTU AND KABILA KEEP MANDELA WAITING.
newsitem.headline: ZAIRE'S MOBUTU AND KABILA KEEP MANDELA WAITING.

text.p: South Africa's Nelson Mandela waited in vain on board ship for a second day on Saturday for Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila to show up for on-off peace talks.
There was no official word when the two Zairean leaders would arrive, though they had been expected in the afternoon.
Mobutu was on land in Congo's port of Pointe Noire while Kabila was said by South African officials to be in the Angolan port on Soyo.
In the Zairean capital Kinshasa, its military governor urged residents to stay calm in the face of rebel advances and told the security forces to protect its population without discrimination.
South African officials told reporters on the SAS Outeniqua that all obstacles to the talks had been removed and that Kabila's arrival from Soyo was imminent.
But as the hours ticked by, Mobutu remained on land while Kabila failed to appear.

On the battlefront, Kabila's rebels drew closer to Kinshasa on several fronts, capturing Mobutu's Lisala birthplace and moving into Kenge just 200 km (125 miles) from the capital, witnesses and security sources said.
The rebels themselves said they were even nearer.

On the humanitarian front, the U.N. flew home more Rwandan Hutu refugees from rebel-held northeastern Zaire, taking the total repatriated in the airlift to 3,902, but torrential rain added to the woes of thousands stuck in makeshift camps.
"President Mandela is willing to stay as long as possible," South African deputy foreign minister, Aziz Pahad, told journalists on board the Outeniqua.
Kabila, who remained in Angola's capital Luanda on Friday while Mandela and Mobutu sailed into international waters to meet him, criticised security and negotiating arrangements.
South African officials said security on the Outeniqua had been tightened to meet Kabila's concerns, with particular attention to Mobutu's bodyguards and the size of delegations.
Mobutu boarded the Russian-built Outeniqua in Pointe Noire with great difficulty on Friday. Unable to climb 31 steep steps, he was driven on board five hours late up a make-shift ramp.
Aged 66 and suffering from prostate cancer, he is one of Africa's most enduring strongmen, backed during the Cold War by the United States as a bulwark against Soviet communism.
He has dominated Zaire since seizing power in 1965 but his illness and the whirlwind rebel offensive have weakened his grip on the former Belgian colony.
Kabila's rebels, who took up arms in October, now control around three quarters of Zaire.
Mobutu aides say talks will focus on a peaceful transition with elections open to all. They reject suggestions that the meeting is a face-saver to allow him to stand down with dignity.
Kabila, 56, says Mobutu must go and has refused to declare a truce for the talks.
The United States, France, Belgium and Britain have troops across the Zaire River in Congo's capital Brazzaville to evacuate their nationals from Kinshasa if need be.
